title: Disinformation and fake news
subtitle: Lying in the age of virality
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: False information spreads 6 times faster than the truth on social media. Why does it, and how can you protect yourself?

hero.hook: An MIT study found that fake news travels 6 times faster than the truth on Twitter. Here is why.

blocks.text: Lying to serve a political goal is nothing new, and there are traces of it from antiquity onward. But the Internet and social media changed the game: false information no longer flows only from a state down to its people, it now spreads sideways, from citizen to citizen.

That shift created a world where truth can look optional next to virality. Understanding how **disinformation** spreads, and who profits from it, has become essential to keeping trust between citizens.

sections.title: Why a lie travels faster than the truth

blocks.text: Disinformation, spread on purpose to manipulate, is not the same thing as an honest mistake. The success of these falsehoods rests on what researchers call the **attention economy**: social media algorithms are built to maximize time spent in front of a screen, and our brains react far more strongly to emotion and shock than to nuance.
A 2018 study by [[MIT]] showed that false stories spread about 6 times faster than verified information on Twitter, because they feel newer and hit harder emotionally.

Algorithms also lock users inside [[filter bubbles]], showing them only content that confirms the opinions they already hold. Someone convinced by a conspiracy theory then reads every new piece of false information as one more proof, which makes any later correction very hard.

sections.title: An industry of lies, between states and profit

blocks.text: Disinformation has become a real industry. States such as Russia, through the Internet Research Agency, created thousands of automated fake accounts to stoke tension inside Western democracies, without even defending one side in particular. The goal is often to create chaos and to make people believe that “everyone lies.”

blocks.caption: False information spreads across social media in seconds

blocks.text: There is also a purely commercial side. In the town of Veles, in North Macedonia, young entrepreneurs built sensationalist websites in 2016 with no political conviction at all, purely to make money from the traffic social media sent them. The lie becomes a profitable product like any other.

sections.title: How to tell the true from the false

blocks.text: Faced with the flood, the news world is organizing. **Fact-checking**, the systematic verification of claims, has become a journalistic discipline in its own right. Agencies such as [[AFP]] and specialized newsrooms use reverse image search tools to spot fakes and analyze suspicious content.

But the race between attack and defense remains uneven. The arrival of [[Deepfakes]], videos faked by artificial intelligence that can put any words in anyone's mouth with unsettling realism, makes telling true from false harder and harder for an untrained eye.

sections.title: Rebuilding trust in a world of images

blocks.text: The long-term effect of disinformation runs deep. People now speak of a **post-truth** era, where objective facts sometimes weigh less than emotion and personal belief. That general relativism weakens the trust we need to face global challenges together, from climate to public health.

The strongest answer is still media education: learning to check a source, to compare several accounts, and to understand how algorithms work. Some also count on content certification technology, which would prove where a video came from the moment it was made. Until then, each person's own vigilance is the first line of defense.

False information spreads on average 6 times faster than the truth on social media, because it feeds on our emotions and our appetite for novelty. Against deepfakes and troll farms, media education remains the best weapon for protecting collective trust.
